CausalChain: Green tea catechin (EGCG) intake -> Direct inhibition of PI3K/AKT and NF-κB/MAPK/EGFR pathways and metal ion chelation/redox modulation -> Induction of precise epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone modifications, microRNA regulation) -> Reprogramming of cancer stem cells to a less aggressive phenotype -> Enhanced apoptosis and increased chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that EGCG, beyond its well-established direct anticancer effects through inhibition of the PI3K/AKT and NF-κB/MAPK/EGFR pathways and antioxidant activity, additionally triggers precise, redox- and metal-ion mediated epigenetic modifications in cancer stem cells. These modifications—including changes in DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA profiles—reprogram the cancer stem cells into a less aggressive phenotype, ultimately rendering them more vulnerable to apoptosis and synergizing with standard chemotherapeutic treatments. To validate this model, we will apply contemporary techniques including high-resolution epigenomic mapping, single-cell multi-omics, and CRISPR-interference approaches to unravel the specific molecular events linking EGCG-induced redox and metal-ion modulation to epigenetic reprogramming in defined cancer stem cell populations.
Abstract: This study proposes that epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), a major green tea catechin, exerts multi-faceted anticancer effects by integrating direct inhibition of key oncogenic pathways with a refined mechanism of epigenetic reprogramming in cancer stem cells. EGCG not only impairs proliferative and survival signaling (e.g., via PI3K/AKT, NF-κB/MAPK/EGFR) but also modulates intracellular redox balance and metal-ion homeostasis, which in turn triggers specific epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation shifts, histone modification alterations, and microRNA regulation. These epigenetic changes are proposed to reprogram cancer stem cells toward a less aggressive phenotype with enhanced apoptotic susceptibility and improved responsiveness to chemotherapeutic agents. The hypothesis leverages advanced technologies including high-resolution epigenomic mapping, CRISPR-based pathway perturbation, and single-cell multi-omics to dissect and validate the underlying molecular events.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis suggested that EGCG reprograms cancer stem cells via epigenetic modifications induced by redox and metal-ion mediated signaling pathways, leading to increased chemosensitivity and apoptosis. The refined hypothesis retains this core idea but integrates direct inhibition of oncogenic pathways (PI3K/AKT, NF-κB/MAPK/EGFR) – already supported by literature – and emphasizes the need for precise mechanistic details. The new version specifies the types of epigenetic modifications involved and outlines a practical experimental framework leveraging modern technologies such as CRISPR screens and single-cell multi-omics. Each step of the original causal chain is maintained: EGCG intake initiates redox and metal-ion modulation that, together with direct pathway inhibition, induces targeted epigenetic changes, thereby reprogramming cancer stem cells and enhancing apoptosis and chemosensitivity.
